title: Khamenei’s Reluctant Approval Fuels Debate as U.S.-Iran Talks Begin
summary: In a rare public statement, Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei revealed his reluctance about the historic memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the United States, writing simply: “I, as a matter of principle, held a different view.” Yet he approved the deal after President Masoud Pezeshkian accepted responsibility. The statement, released Thursday, is Khamenei’s only public reaction since becoming supreme leader in March — he has not been seen or heard from since. On Sunday, senior negotiators from both nations met in Switzerland, mediated by Pakistan and Qatar, to advance the 60-day roadmap aimed at ending the war that began with U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on February 28. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi led Iran’s team; Vice President JD Vance headed the U.S. delegation. But back in Tehran, the deal is under fire. The director of state TV’s main news channel resigned after it aired an 11-minute interview with hardline cleric Mahmoud Nabavian, who claimed Khamenei opposed the April 8 ceasefire and wanted immediate enforcement of a toll system for ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz, plus “exclusive management” of the waterway, war reparations, and no nuclear concessions. The interview was abruptly cut and later vanished from the online archive. Pezeshkian called the MoU a “historic document” reflecting national dignity. The Supreme National Security Council said it safeguards Iran’s rights while honoring leaders killed in the war — including Khamenei’s father, former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who died on the first day of attacks. Almost all council members, including military commanders, voted yes; only ultra-hardliner Saeed Jalili voted no, arguing the deal fails Iran’s “national interests.” Hardline factions are weaponizing state media. One TV program demanded Tehran’s Mehrabad Airport be closed to prevent negotiators from leaving. Meanwhile, Iran’s military said the Strait of Hormuz was closed again due to Israeli strikes on Lebanon, though the U.S. military insists it remains open. The first priority in Switzerland, Iran’s foreign ministry stressed, is enforcing the deal — especially in Lebanon — before technical talks on a long-term resolution.
why_it_matters: This deal, and the internal power struggle it reveals, could decide whether a wider war ignites — unsettling global oil supplies, international security, and the future of diplomacy in one of the world’s most volatile regions.

background_read: The United States and Iran have not had full diplomatic relations since 1980, after the Iranian Revolution overthrew the U.S.-backed Shah. Tensions have simmered for decades over Iran’s nuclear program, regional influence, and sanctions.

The Strait of Hormuz (a narrow water passage between Iran and Oman) is one of the world’s most important oil routes — about a fifth of global oil passes through it. Threats to close it can send fuel prices soaring worldwide.

Iran’s political system blends elected offices like the presidency with unelected religious authority. The Supreme Leader (currently Mojtaba Khamenei, who succeeded his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in March 2024) has the final say on major state decisions.

The war mentioned began with U.S.-Israeli airstrikes on February 28, 2024, escalating quickly. A fragile ceasefire was reached on April 8, but disputes over enforcement, especially in Lebanon, have kept tensions high.

└─ AIM: Advance a 60-day roadmap to end the war

perspectives.description: Supporters see the MoU as a historic chance to end a devastating war and avoid direct confrontation with the U.S. They argue that accepting the deal protects Iran’s national dignity while honoring the late supreme leader. President Pezeshkian’s team frames it as a necessary compromise that could lead to eased sanctions and economic recovery.

Ultra-hardliners like Saeed Jalili and cleric Nabavian believe the agreement sells out Iran’s interests by not demanding enough concessions from the West. They want immediate control over the Strait of Hormuz and heavy war reparations, and they see any nuclear compromise as a betrayal. They are using state media to drum up public anger and delegitimize the deal.

The standoff reflects a long-running structural tension in Iran’s system: elected officials often push for pragmatic engagement, while unelected hardline bodies can veto or sabotage such moves. The fact that Khamenei allowed the deal despite personal dissent suggests he is balancing factions, but the episode also exposes how fragile top-level consensus really is.

The immediate test is whether the Swiss talks can produce concrete enforcement in Lebanon. If the hardliners succeed in undermining the process, the war could re-intensify — with disastrous humanitarian and economic consequences. A more stable outcome would require not only a ceasefire but also a clear path to addressing the deep grievances on both sides, including regional security arrangements for strategic waterways.
